def: A neural network, usually a transformer with billions of parameters, trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. Chat assistants are LLMs with extra fine-tuning.
The task an LLM is trained on and runs: given the text so far, give every possible next token a probability. Generation repeats it one token at a time.
The neural network architecture behind modern LLMs (2017): stacked blocks of attention and MLP layers that process all tokens in parallel.
The function $p_i = e^{z_i} / \sum_j e^{z_j}$ that turns raw scores (logits) into probabilities that are positive and add up to 1.
A model after pretraining only. It continues text well but does not reliably follow instructions until it is fine-tuned.
Giving a model the facts it needs in its context, such as retrieved documents or tool results, so its answer rests on real sources rather than on what merely sounds likely.
A number inside a model that training adjusts, such as a weight or a bias. Model size is quoted as a parameter count.
A function that turns how wrong a model's predictions are into a single number to minimise. Language models use cross-entropy on the next token.
The loss $-\ln p$ of the probability a model gave to the correct class or token, averaged over examples. It heavily penalises confident wrong predictions.
An optimisation method that repeatedly moves each parameter a small step against the gradient of the loss: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \, \partial L / \partial w$.
The algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter by applying the chain rule backwards from the output, layer by layer.
A unit of text from a model's fixed vocabulary, often a word or a piece of a word, identified by an integer ID.
A tokenizer-training method that starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new vocabulary entry.
A learned vector of numbers that represents a token or a piece of text, placed so that similar items have nearby vectors.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors, $a \cdot b / (\|a\| \|b\|)$, ranging from $-1$ to $1$. Used to compare embeddings regardless of their length.
The operation where each token computes weights over the other tokens from query-key dot products and takes a weighted sum of their value vectors.
A mask that sets attention scores for future positions to $-\infty$ before softmax, so each token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens.
Running several attention operations in parallel on slices of width $d_h = d/h$, so different heads can learn different patterns, then concatenating and projecting the results.
Adding a sub-layer's input to its output, $x + F(x)$, which keeps a direct path for information and gradients through deep networks.
A divisor applied to logits before softmax. Values below 1 sharpen the next-token distribution; values above 1 flatten it.
Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least $p$, after renormalising them.
The exponential of the average negative log-probability a model assigns to the actual tokens. Lower means the model predicts the text better.

Stored key and value vectors for all previous tokens at every layer, reused at each generation step so they are not recomputed. Its size is $2 \cdot L \cdot h_{kv} \cdot d_h$ times bytes per value, per token.
Fluent model output that is false or not supported by the given sources, arising because the model generates probable text rather than verified text.
A GPU machine or container rented by the hour from a cloud marketplace. It bills for every second it is running, busy or idle, and its storage volume usually keeps billing until deleted.

Memory for the intermediate tensors the forward pass keeps so the backward pass can compute gradients. It grows with the tokens per micro-batch (B·n), the model's width and depth, and the vocabulary size of the logits.
A PyTorch build without CUDA libraries, installed from PyTorch's CPU package index; it is far smaller than the CUDA build and is all a machine without an NVIDIA GPU can use.
A self-contained folder with its own Python interpreter and installed packages, created with `python -m venv` or conda, so one project's pinned versions cannot break another's.

A vector that tells the model where a token sits in the sequence, added to the token embedding because attention by itself ignores order. It can be a learned table or a fixed pattern of sines and cosines.
Rescales each token vector to mean 0 and variance 1 across its features, then applies a learned scale and shift. It keeps activations in a stable range inside transformer blocks.

The block layout x + sublayer(LayerNorm(x)), where normalisation is applied to the input of each sublayer instead of after the residual add. It leaves a clean identity path through the network and trains more stably than the original post-norm layout.
The Gaussian Error Linear Unit, x times the standard normal CDF of x. A smooth alternative to ReLU used in GPT-style feed-forward networks.
The per-token sublayer of a transformer block: widen each vector (usually to 4d), apply a nonlinearity, and project back to d. It holds about two thirds of each block's parameters.

A tokenizer whose token IDs are the raw UTF-8 bytes of the text, giving a fixed vocabulary of 256. It can encode any text but produces longer sequences than sub-word tokenizers, especially for non-Latin scripts.

Building next-token targets by moving the input sequence one position to the left, so the target at each position is the token that follows it. It must happen exactly once, in either the data pipeline or the model.
The Adam optimiser with weight decay applied directly to the weights instead of through the gradient. It is the standard optimiser for training transformers.
Scaling the whole gradient down when its overall norm exceeds a threshold, so one unusual batch cannot produce a huge update. The direction of the gradient is unchanged.
The loss measured on held-out data that is never used for gradient updates. Comparing it with the training loss shows whether a model is learning general patterns or memorising.

A sampling rule that keeps only the k most likely next tokens, renormalises their probabilities and samples from them. Unlike top-p, the number of candidates is fixed regardless of how confident the model is.

A normalisation layer that divides each token's vector by its root-mean-square and multiplies by a learned gain, without subtracting the mean or adding a bias. It is cheaper than LayerNorm and used by Llama-family models.
A way of encoding position by rotating pairs of query and key coordinates by angles proportional to the token's position. The resulting attention score depends only on the distance between tokens.

A gated feed-forward layer that multiplies a SiLU-activated gate projection element-wise with a second projection before projecting back down. Its hidden size is usually about 8d/3 so it has the same parameters as a 4d GELU layer.
Attention in which each token may only attend to the most recent W tokens. It caps the KV cache and per-step cost, while stacked layers still pass information from further back.
The first few tokens of a sequence, on which attention heads learn to park surplus softmax weight. Keeping them in the cache is what lets a sliding-window model stream without collapsing.
A fixed-size KV cache that writes each new token into slot position mod W, overwriting the oldest entry. Memory stays constant no matter how long generation runs.

Summing the gradients of several small micro-batches before one optimizer step, so a large effective batch fits in limited memory. Each micro-batch loss is divided by the number of micro-batches so the sum equals the big-batch mean.

Multiplying the loss by a large factor before the backward pass in FP16 training so small gradients do not underflow to zero, then dividing the gradients back before the update. Dynamic loss scaling lowers the factor on overflow and raises it after a run of clean steps.
Raising the learning rate from near zero to its peak over the first steps of training, so the optimizer's early, poorly estimated updates stay small.

A snapshot on disk that is enough to resume training exactly: weights, optimizer state, scheduler and scaler state, step count, random-number-generator state and data position. It is about three times the size of a weights-only file with AdamW.
The fraction of the hardware's peak FLOP rate a training run actually uses, estimated as 6 × parameters × tokens per second divided by peak FLOP/s.
Cross-entropy expressed per byte of text instead of per token, which makes models with different tokenizers comparable. It equals loss per token divided by (ln 2 × average bytes per token).
A layer with many parallel feed-forward networks (experts) and a router that sends each token to only a few of them. It raises total parameters without raising compute per token.
The parameters a single token actually passes through in an MoE model: the shared layers plus the k chosen experts per layer. They set compute per token, while total parameters set memory.
The small linear layer in an MoE layer that scores every expert for each token, keeps the top k, and turns their probabilities into mixing weights.

An auxiliary loss added during MoE training that is smallest when tokens are spread evenly across experts. The Switch Transformer version is N times the sum over experts of token fraction times mean router probability.
The maximum number of tokens one expert processes per batch, set by a capacity factor times its fair share. Tokens beyond it are dropped and pass through on the residual connection.
Placing different experts of an MoE layer on different devices and moving tokens to them and back with all-to-all communication.
